entry.title: Slack Water, the new EP
entry.content:
Slack Water is the twenty minutes between tides when nothing moves. These four tracks were built from recordings made in that window, once a month for a year.

Tracklist

  1. Second Mooring Post (5:12)
  2. Bait Shop Radio (4:03)
  3. Fenders (6:40)
  4. Slack Water (8:21)

Mastered at the boathouse. Tape edition of 100, download everywhere else.

entry.title: The harbour at low tide
entry.content:
Twice a day the water leaves, and the harbour shows you its bones: the chains, the old tyres hung as fenders, the steps worn into a bowl by two hundred years of boots.

At low tide you can walk out to the second mooring post. Nobody tells you this. You learn it by watching the boy who sells bait, who learned it from someone else.

What the mud keeps

A spoon, a bicycle bell, the brass plate from a boat that sank before anyone now living was born. The mud keeps everything and gives it back slowly.

The harbour is not a place. It is a schedule that happens to have walls.

I go down most evenings now. The light is better than any photograph of it.
entry.summary: Twice a day the water leaves and the town shows you how it is held together.

entry.title: Keeping a commonplace book
entry.content:
A commonplace book is a notebook of things worth keeping: quotations, sums, recipes, the name of a bolt. I have kept one for nineteen years.1 This is how it works, in more detail than anyone needs.

The rules

  1. Write the date before anything else.
  2. Copy quotations by hand, with the page number.
  3. Never tear out a page; cross it out instead.
  4. Index the book when it is full, not before.

Paper - a plain A5 notebook with numbered pages.

Pen - whatever is in the coat pocket.

Index - the last four pages, alphabetical, by subject.

A worked example

Here is the index format I settled on after many bad ones:

Subject Pages Notes
Tides 4, 17, 52 tables copied from the harbour office
Radios 9, 10 valve numbers, a wiring sketch
Bread 33 a recipe from a neighbour

When the book moved to a computer I wrote a tiny script to rebuild the index:

import re

def index(lines):
    entries = {}
    for page, line in lines:
        for tag in re.findall(r"#(\w+)", line):
            entries.setdefault(tag, []).append(page)
    return dict(sorted(entries.items()))

The script lives in the back of the book too, written out by hand.2

Whatever you copy out, you keep twice: once on the page and once in the hand.

What it is for

Mostly it is for remembering where I read something. Sometimes it is for noticing that I have copied the same sentence three times in ten years, which tells me more about myself than any diary.

  1. The first one was a school exercise book with a broken spine. ↩

  2. Yes, this is a little absurd. ↩
entry.summary: A long note on the oldest writing tool I use, with the system that keeps it useful.

entry.title: A ledger of small repairs
entry.content:
For one year I wrote down every repair I made. There were one hundred and four. Most took less than ten minutes. Three took most of a weekend.

The ledger is not interesting because of the repairs. It is interesting because of the pattern: things break where people touch them.
entry.summary: One year of fixing things, written down: what broke, what it cost, what it taught.
